newsitem.title: CROATIA: POLITICS HALTING CROATIA CREDIT UPGRADE-MERRILL.
newsitem.headline: POLITICS HALTING CROATIA CREDIT UPGRADE-MERRILL.

text.p: Worsening relations between Croatia and the international community could prevent the country from winning an investment rating upgrade in the near future, U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch said.
And the recent postponement of part of an IMF loan had also had negative market reaction, the bank said in its August Emerging Markets Debt Monthly research note.

Merrill Lynch said ratings agencies believed Croatia merited a significantly higher rating in terms of its economic performance and were not unduly concerned about the worsening of political relations with the international community.
But it added: "Developments do, however, reduce the prospect of any upgrade in the ratings in the near future".

James Droop at IBCA rating agency echoed this. "It is the political factors that mean Croatia is not rated higher than it is at the moment...There has been a slight worsening with the delay of the IMF and World Bank loans," he told Reuters.

However he said the political factors had been around since the country was first rated in January and there was no question of a downgrade at the moment. IBCA, the European rating agency, awarded Croatia a BBB minus.
Croatia is currently rated at the bottom of the investment grade ladder, carrying a Baa3 from Moody's and a BBB- from Standard & Poors.

A recent widening in the spread of Croatian Eurobonds compared to the benchmark U.S. treasury bond was a negative market reaction to the July decision by the International Monetary Fund to postpone a loan to Croatia because of political considerations, Merrill Lynch said.

Croatian Eurobonds due to mature in 2002 are now trading at a spread of 128 basis points over the U.S. compared to around 80 basis points for the comparable Hungarian 2002 bond and 83 for the Polish 2004 bond, it added.

"Although IMF funds are not needed either for the balance of payments or for the budget, this is clearly a negative development. Spreads are now the widest for any investment grade country," the bank said.
It said it did not agree with rating agencies that Croatia was as good a credit risk as Poland and Hungary, but it did not believe such a large differential was justified.
The bank assisted the former Yugoslav republic to win its investment grade credit ratings and arranged bond issues.

The IMF in July delayed the release of $40 million, the second tranche of a $486 million three-year loan to Croatia, to put pressure on Zagreb to live up to commitments it made in the Dayton peace treaty that ended the Bosnian war in 1995.

Those commitments involve handing over indicted war criminals to the international tribunal in The Hague, guaranteeing the safe return of thousands of Serb refugees to Croatia and releasing the government's grip on the media.

The United States put strong pressure on the IMF to postpone the tranche even though Zagreb had fulfilled all economic conditions set out under the loan agreement. Some European and other nations were concerned the decision could lead to the politicisation of the fund.
The IMF decision came after the World Bank also delayed considering new loans for Croatia.
Merrill Lynch also highlighted Croatia's widening current account gap and said the trend deterioration was a "long term cause of concern".

Exports for the January-June period rose 2.3 percent year on year compared to 1996 while imports rose by 19.1 percent, the state statistics bureau said. In June exports were up 19.2 percent year on year while imports rose 33 percent. -- Zagreb newsroom +385 1 455 7075
